content: Platanus is a genus of trees native to the Northern Hemisphere and represents the only living members of the family Platanaceae. These trees are typically tall, reaching heights of 30 to 50 meters. With the exception of Platanus kerrii, all species are deciduous. They are commonly found in riparian or wetland habitats in the wild, although they demonstrate drought tolerance when cultivated. The hybrid London Plane is particularly well-suited to urban environments. In English, these trees are often referred to as planes or plane trees. In North America, some species, such as Platanus occidentalis, are called sycamores, though this term can also refer to other unrelated species like Ficus sycomorus or Acer pseudoplatanus. The flowers of Platanus are small and arranged in spherical clusters known as globose heads. Each flower has 3 to 7 hairy sepals, which may be fused at the base, and 3 to 7 spatulate petals. The trees are monoecious, meaning male and female flowers are found on the same plant but in separate structures. The number of flower heads in a cluster varies by species. Male flowers contain 3 to 8 stamens, while female flowers have a superior ovary with 3 to 7 carpels. Male flower heads fall off after releasing their pollen. Once pollinated, female flowers develop into achenes, which aggregate into a ball-like structure. These fruiting balls are 2.5 to 4 cm in diameter and contain hundreds of achenes, each with a single seed. The achenes are equipped with stiff, yellow-green bristles that aid in wind dispersal, similar to dandelions. The leaves of Platanus are simple and, in the subgenus Platanus, have a palmate shape. The base of the leaf stalk (petiole) is enlarged and completely encloses the young stem bud, which becomes visible only after the leaf falls. The bark of these trees exfoliates easily, peeling off in irregular patches to create a mottled, scaly appearance. On older trunks, the bark may thicken and crack instead of flaking off. The genus Platanus is divided into two subgenera: Castaneophyllum, which includes the unique P. kerrii, and Platanus, which contains all other species. Recent genetic studies have expanded the number of recognized species within the subgenus Platanus. Evidence suggests that P. racemosa is more closely related to P. orientalis than to other North American species. Fossil records indicate that plane trees have existed for at least 115 million years, dating back to the Lower Cretaceous period. Despite the geographic separation between North America and the Old World, species from these regions can hybridize and produce fertile offspring, such as the London Plane. Platanus trees are susceptible to several diseases. Plane Anthracnose, caused by the fungus Apiognomonia veneta, can lead to significant defoliation, particularly during cold, wet springs. American species like P. occidentalis are the most vulnerable, while P. orientalis is the most resistant. The hybrid London Plane exhibits intermediate resistance. Another serious disease, caused by the fungus Ceratocystis platani, has become a major issue in Europe, leading to wilt in affected trees. Other diseases, such as powdery mildew, are common but less severe. Additionally, Platanus species serve as host plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera, including Phyllonorycter platani. The primary use of Platanus trees is as ornamental plants, particularly in urban areas and along roadsides. The London Plane is especially popular for this purpose. In some cases, the American plane is cultivated for timber, and research has been conducted into its potential as a biomass crop. The oriental plane (P. orientalis) is widely used as an ornamental tree and has minor medicinal applications. Culturally, Platanus orientalis holds significant historical importance, particularly in the Old World.
